name: Guinness Storehouse
label: Guinness Storehouse
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'St. James's Gate' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'St James's Gate Medical' (node/10792934890): point; moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/44597908: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Guinness Storehouse' (72 m across).

text.description:
The Guinness Storehouse is the visitor centre at St. James's Gate Brewery, and it is one of the best-known sights in Dublin. The building went up in 1902 as a fermentation plant, in the style of the Chicago School of architecture. It was the first multi-storey steel-framed building in Ireland. It opened to visitors on 2 December 2000 and has since welcomed over twenty million people. Inside, seven floors wrap around a glass atrium shaped like a pint of Guinness, and the top floor has the Gravity Bar with views over Dublin.

For a free photo, the best spot is outside, in front of the Guinness gate beside the Storehouse. The brand sign sits across the entrance and the brewery buildings fill the space behind it, so one frame tells you where you are. It is at the corner where Robert Street, Market Street South and Belview meet. The Storehouse itself is a ticketed attraction, so check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside.

Keep the shot simple. Stand square to the gate so the sign reads clearly, and let the brewery buildings sit behind as the backdrop. If other visitors are posing, wait a moment and a gap usually opens. Inside, the Gravity Bar gives rooftop views rather than a view of the building, so it makes a different kind of photo.
text.geographic_location: The Guinness Storehouse is inside St. James's Gate Brewery, west of Dublin city centre, on Market Street South. The gate for the photo is at the corner where Market Street South, Robert Street and Belview meet, beside the Storehouse.
text.directions_text: From James's (Luas Red Line) the Storehouse is about 440 m to the east. From Fatima (Luas Red Line) the Storehouse is about 539 m to the north-east. Head for the corner where Robert Street, Market Street South and Belview meet, beside the Storehouse. The phone icon on the map marks the spot. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the gates, the sign and the buildings behind. If you are close and the gates will not fit, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep the phone level so the edges do not lean. If your phone has telephoto (2x or more), use it for a tighter shot of the sign.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject, at the corner where Robert Street, Market Street South and Belview meet (the phone icon on the map), in front of the brewery gate beside the Storehouse. The photo shows the gate and its Guinness sign, with the brewery buildings behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the gates up square so the sign sits near the centre. Include a little of the brewery buildings above the gates for context. For a different view, the Gravity Bar inside gives panoramic views over the Dublin rooftops, though it is ticketed and does not show the building's exterior.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sign to set focus, then nudge the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the gates keep their detail. Take a few shots in case people walk through the frame. Inside, photography is allowed without flash or tripods.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go in daylight so the sign is easy to read. Outside the busiest part of the day you are more likely to get the gates with fewer people in front.

text.access_note: The gates can be photographed from the street for free, but the Storehouse itself is a ticketed attraction, so check the official site before you go.

name: Trinity College: Front Square and the Long Room
label: Trinity College
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Fellows' Square' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Fellows' Square' (relation/4616154): middle (72 m across).

text.description: Trinity College is Ireland's oldest university, founded in 1592 by Queen Elizabeth I, and its old courtyards are a major part of a destination that receives over two million visitors a year. The 18th-century Parliament Square, often called Front Square, holds the freestanding Campanile. The Old Library was begun in 1712 and has housed the Book of Kells since 1661. Inside it, the Long Room is a 65-metre barrel-vaulted hall with two storeys of oak bookcases and marble busts in the niches. The grounds receive over two million visitors a year, so the main courtyards can be busy. For a calmer view, this map sends you to Fellows' Square, a quieter open-air courtyard. From here you get a wider look at the historic quadrangles, with the old library building across the lawns. Cobbles, lawns, stone façades and the Campanile give you plenty of layers to work with. Inside the Long Room, flash is prohibited and the Book of Kells itself may not be photographed. A conservation project has moved most of the books into storage, so the shelves may look emptier than in older photos. Take your wide shot here first, then walk over to Front Square for the Campanile.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Dublin, on the Trinity College campus beside College Green. The Front Square lies a short walk inside the college grounds.
text.directions_text: Take the Luas Green Line to the Trinity Luas stop; the college lies to the south of the stop, about 2 minutes on foot. Westmoreland Luas stop, also on the Luas Green Line, is about 4 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole quadrangle, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the old library building or the Campanile.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Fellows' Square. A wider view of the college's historic quadrangles, with the old library building visible across the lawns. Front Square, the usual busy spot, is to the north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the buildings' vertical lines straight to stop them leaning. Put the lawn or cobbles in the lower third and the old library across the middle. As an alternative, walk to Front Square and frame the Campanile with the surrounding buildings and open ground around it. A panorama works well across the quadrangles if you pan slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and pale stone keep their detail. In the Long Room, switch the flash off, as it is prohibited, and hold the phone steady using the 1x lens.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Try going early or later in the day, when the courtyards tend to be quieter. Check the official site for visiting times before you go.

text.access_note: The courtyards are open-air parts of the campus, but the Long Room is inside a ticketed attraction (the Book of Kells exhibition), so check the official site before you go.

name: Kilmainham Gaol
label: Kilmainham Gaol
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kilmainham Gaol East Wing central atrium' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/3950323926: the OpenStreetMap point 'Kilmainham Jail Museum'.

text.description:
Kilmainham Gaol is a former prison in west Dublin, now run as a museum by the Office of Public Works. It opened in 1796 as the "New Gaol" and was officially the County of Dublin Gaol. It is best known for holding Irish revolutionaries, including the leaders of the 1916 Easter Rising, several of whom were executed here. The prison was decommissioned in 1924 and was later saved from demolition by a restoration society formed in 1958.

For photographs, the Victorian East Wing is the big draw. Standing on the floor of the central atrium, you look up at tiers of cells and iron walkways rising on every side beneath a skylight. The lines run in near-perfect symmetry towards the middle, which makes a strong, simple picture even on a phone. Guides often describe it as the most photographed part of the gaol.

Access to the East Wing needs a paid tour or ticket, so plan ahead. The museum's photo rules are reported as allowing photos without flash, and tripods are not allowed. Look out for signs inside in case anything has changed. Keep your phone steady, give other visitors room, and leave the flash off. The space is also a solemn one, so a quiet, respectful approach suits it.
text.geographic_location: Kilmainham Gaol is in Kilmainham, a district of Dublin to the west of the city centre. The nearest Luas stops are on the Red Line, a short walk to the south.
text.directions_text: Take the Luas Red Line to Suir Road. The gaol is about 600 m on foot from there, to the north. Goldenbridge, also on the Luas Red Line, is an alternative, about 730 m on foot with the gaol to the north-east. Once inside, follow the tour or the staff to the East Wing. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the atrium. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want to fit in the full height of the cell tiers and the skylight, since you cannot step back far.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the photo shows rows of cell tiers and iron walkways rising around the open space under the skylight.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the central vertical with the middle of the atrium, so the walkways converge evenly on both sides. Tilt the phone up slowly until the skylight sits near the top of the frame. For a different view, the entrance façade with the tricolour and the open sky above Stonebreakers' Yard with the memorial cross are also worth a photo.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the cells to focus, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the bright skylight does not wash out. Keep the flash off. Hold the phone with both hands and brace your elbows against your body for a steadier shot. Night mode may switch on in the dim light, so stay still for a moment while it works.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when light enters from above. Tour times are set by the site, so check the official site before you go.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed museum and the East Wing needs a paid tour or ticket, so check the official site before you go for current times and photo rules.

name: Dublin Castle
label: Dublin Castle
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Upper Castle Yard' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Upper Castle Yard' (way/292056033): middle (113 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/350242806: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Dublin Castle' (373 m across).

text.description:
Dublin Castle is far more of a palace than a fortress today, and that contrast is what makes it fun to photograph. A castle has stood here since the early 13th century. It was founded in 1204 on the orders of King John, on the high ground beside the dark pool (Dubh Linn) that gave Dublin its name. After a serious fire in 1684 it was rebuilt, and most of what you see now is Georgian. The Record Tower, from around 1228 to 1230, is the only tower left from the original fortress.

The classic picture is taken in Upper Castle Yard. Stand in the cobbled courtyard and frame the Bedford Tower, with its clock stage and copper cupola, centred between the Gates of Fortitude and Justice. The symmetry does most of the work for you. If you have time, two other spots give very different views. Dubhlinn Gardens shows the Georgian ranges of the castle with a lawn in front. Lower Castle Yard puts the medieval Record Tower beside the neo-Gothic Chapel Royal, with its carved stone heads, so several centuries of building sit in one frame.

The castle is still used for state occasions, including presidential inaugurations, so keep an eye out for staff and closed areas while you shoot.
text.geographic_location: Dublin Castle stands off Dame Street in central Dublin, on the highest ground in the city centre. The complex also contains the Chester Beatty Library and its gardens.
text.directions_text: From Jervis (Luas Red Line), the castle is about 550 m away, to the south. From St. Stephen's Green (Luas Green Line), it is about 560 m away, to the north-west. Enter the castle from Dame Street and walk through to Upper Castle Yard. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the tower framed between the two gates. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the courtyard feels too tight to fit everything in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Upper Castle Yard. Bedford Tower with its clock stage and copper cupola, framed between the Gates of Fortitude and Justice across the cobbled courtyard.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with the centre column so the two gates balance on either side. Hold the phone level so the walls don't lean. For a different view, try Dubhlinn Gardens for the Georgian ranges over the lawn, or Lower Castle Yard for the Record Tower beside the Chapel Royal.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky doesn't wash out the copper cupola. Use 2x for a close shot of the clock stage rather than cropping later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is recommended for the classic shot of the tower between the gates.

text.access_note: The castle is a working State complex and parts of the grounds can close for official events, so check dublincastle.ie (the official site) before you go.

name: Grafton Street
label: Grafton Street
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Molly Malone statue' (3 web pages); placed at crossing of Suffolk Street and Andrew Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q135501: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description: Grafton Street is one of Dublin's two main shopping streets, running from St Stephen's Green down to College Green. It grew from a country lane that was widened from 1708, and its line was shaped by a small river that now runs underground. It is named after Charles FitzRoy, 2nd Duke of Grafton, who owned land here. Most of the street has been pedestrian-only since 1982. That helps a lot with photos, because you can step back and take in the shopfronts, the crowds and the buskers without cars in the way. The usual place to start is the bronze Molly Malone statue and her cart. She stands on Suffolk Street, just outside the north end of Grafton Street, after being moved from the street itself in 2014. From there the Trinity College area and the start of the street sit close behind her. Take care at this end: the stretch between Nassau Street and College Green is not pedestrianised, and there is traffic and there are Luas tracks. If you walk the street, two good alternatives are Fusiliers' Arch, for a view framed by the gateway, and Bewley's Oriental Café, for a facade shot with shoppers in the frame.
text.geographic_location: Grafton Street is in Dublin city centre, on the Southside. It links College Green and Trinity College in the north with St Stephen's Green in the south.
text.directions_text: From Dawson (Luas Green Line), Grafton Street is to the south-west, about 3 minutes on foot. From St. Stephen's Green (Luas Green Line), the street runs north from the park, about 4 minutes on foot to the point on the map. The Molly Malone statue is at the northern end, so you can also walk the whole street from the park and finish there. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the statue with the street behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole scene, or to telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for tighter shots of the statue or the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Suffolk Street and Andrew Street (statue at the corner, just outside the north end of Grafton Street). The bronze Molly Malone statue and cart in the foreground, with the north end of Grafton Street and the Trinity College area close behind. Grafton Street itself runs away to the south from here.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Keep the statue and cart large in the foreground, and let the start of the street and the buildings fill the background. Turn on gridlines and line the street up with a vertical grid line so the buildings don't lean. For a different view, try Fusiliers' Arch, where the arch frames the street receding into the distance. Bewley's Oriental Café works well for a facade shot with passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statue to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bronze doesn't look washed out against a bright sky. Stay on the pavement, well clear of the road and the Luas tracks, while you frame the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier in the day is usually calmer, with fewer people around the statue. Busy times give you more life in the street scenes.

text.access_note: Grafton Street is an open public street and mostly pedestrian, but the north end has traffic and Luas tram tracks, so stand clear of vehicles.

name: Phoenix Park
label: Phoenix Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Wellington Monument' (5 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Wellington Monument' (way/40498842): middle (64 m across); moved 20 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/4423275: large area 'Phoenix Park' (4924 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: 'phoenix park' alone also means parks in other places.

text.description: Phoenix Park is a large public urban park. Its 11 km wall surrounds 707 hectares of grassland and tree-lined avenues, a short way west of Dublin city centre and north of the River Liffey. A herd of wild fallow deer has lived here since the 17th century, and the park was opened to the people of Dublin in 1745. For a phone photo, the best subject is the Wellington Monument. This granite obelisk is 62 m tall and is described as the largest obelisk in Europe. It rises over grass and works well as a tall vertical shot against the sky. Four bronze plaques at its base were cast from cannon captured at Waterloo, which makes a good close-up detail. The park is huge, so don't try to cover it all. Pick the obelisk, then add one wider shot of the open parkland. If you have time, the Magazine Fort gives raised views over the trees, and the meadow at Fifteen Acres suits wide, open pictures with deer and clusters of trees. Stay well back from the deer and keep clear of the road on Chesterfield Avenue, which carries traffic. Hold the phone upright, use the gridlines to keep the obelisk straight, and leave plenty of sky above the tip.
text.geographic_location: Phoenix Park lies about 2 to 4 km west of Dublin city centre, north of the River Liffey. The Wellington Monument stands inside the park.
text.directions_text: The park lies west of the city centre: from the centre, head west along the north side of the River Liffey. Parkgate Street, just outside the park near Heuston Station, is a handy place to aim for, and from there you can walk into the park. A shuttle bus (Route 99) also runs from there, so check the official site for its current times. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from a little way back so the whole obelisk fits. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) close to the base, pointing up, for a dramatic look, but expect the sides to lean in. Use telephoto (2x-5x) for the bronze plaques or for distant views.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (open lawn around the base of the obelisk). The 62 m granite obelisk rising over open grass, framed for a tall vertical composition against the sky. Check the map before you walk, as the monument is easy to mix up with other points in this large park.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright for a tall composition, with the obelisk straight in the centre or just off it and a good band of grass below. Keep the sky above the tip so it doesn't look cramped. For a different view, the Magazine Fort has raised outlooks over the parkland, which work well with telephoto.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Turn on gridlines to keep the sides of the obelisk straight. Tap the granite to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. At blue hour, use night mode and rest your elbows against your body or a solid surface to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, when the light falls on the granite and the city begins to glow. Blue hour also works for the lit obelisk.

text.access_note: The park itself is open public space, but some places inside it, such as Dublin Zoo, the visitor centre and the Magazine Fort, may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Temple Bar
label: Temple Bar
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ha'penny Bridge' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Ha'penny Bridge' (way/399007550): middle (59 m across); moved 30 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/76592311: large area 'Temple Bar' (809 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: 'temple bar' alone also means London's Temple Bar.

text.description:
Temple Bar is the cobbled, lively patch of central Dublin on the south bank of the River Liffey. It is promoted as the city's cultural quarter, and it is also a busy spot for nightlife. It photographs well because the details are packed close together: narrow streets, string lights, painted pub fronts and the river just behind. The name appears on a map of Dublin from 1673, when the street was newly built on reclaimed riverside land. Fishamble Street, at the area's western edge, saw the first performance of Handel's Messiah in 1742.

For the widest and most rewarding view, start on the Ha'penny Bridge. From the bridge deck you look back across the Liffey. The white cast-iron arch is in the foreground and the lit streets of Temple Bar sit on the far bank behind it. Guides often list the bridge among the city's most photographed places.

From there, walk into the streets for close-ups. The red front of The Temple Bar pub, with its hanging flower baskets and lights, looks best from the street. Love Lane has tiled walls, painted art and handwritten notes, and suits tight detail shots. Evenings are atmospheric but crowded, so dawn or a Sunday morning gives you more space.
text.geographic_location: Temple Bar is on the south bank of the River Liffey in central Dublin (Dublin 2). It is bounded by Westmoreland Street to the east, Fishamble Street to the west and Dame Street to the south.
text.directions_text: The nearest stops are Westmoreland (Luas Green Line), about 264 m to the west of Temple Bar, and Jervis (Luas Red Line), about 292 m to the north-west of Temple Bar. From Jervis, Temple Bar lies to the south-east, across the Liffey. The Ha'penny Bridge is the natural place to start: Temple Bar is about 118 m south of it, on the far bank. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the bridge arch with the Temple Bar streets behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) in the narrow streets, or if the bridge is crowded. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for pub signs, flower baskets and other details from across the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ha'penny Bridge (on the bridge deck, looking back toward the Temple Bar side of the Liffey). The white cast-iron arch over the Liffey with the lit Temple Bar streets on the far bank behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the bridge rail or arch in the foreground, with the Temple Bar buildings behind. Hold the phone level so the buildings do not lean. Once you are in the streets, try The Temple Bar's red pub front as a straight-on shot from across the cobbles. In Love Lane, shoot tight detail shots of the tiles, art and notes rather than the whole alley.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge or the lit buildings to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lights do not wash out. In the evening, let night mode run and brace your elbows on the rail to keep the shot steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dawn or evening works best. Expect crowds from about 6pm on Fridays and Saturdays. Sunday mornings are likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: The bridge and streets are open public space, but the pub front is a commercial venue, so shoot from the street rather than going inside, and check the official site before you go if you plan to visit any venue.
claims_not_in_sources: The bridge and the Temple Bar streets are open public space that can be walked at any time.
Evening is when the string lights and pub lights show up best against the sky.

name: St Stephen's Green
label: St Stephen's Green
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Fusiliers' Arch' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Fusiliers' Arch' (relation/18631966): middle (12 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/18631965: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St Stephen's Green' (557 m across).

text.description: St Stephen's Green is a 22-acre public park in the middle of Dublin, and the largest of the city's Georgian garden squares. For photographs, the best-known view is from the Fusiliers' Arch. From the entrance you look south down the long, tree-lined central path, with the arch framing the shot in the foreground. That gives you a strong frame within a frame, with the path leading the eye into the park. The park has a long history. It was a marshy common until 1663, then closed off for the use of local residents. It was officially re-opened to the public on 27 July 1880 by Lord Ardilaun, in the layout designed by William Sheppard that we see today. The grounds measure roughly 550 by 450 metres, so there is plenty of room to wander once you have your main shot. If you have time, the lake with its stone bridges, waterfowl and flowerbeds makes a quieter alternative to the main path. For the arch view, keep the path in the centre of the frame, keep your phone level, and wait a moment for walkers to space out so the path looks clean. Sunny weekends and lunchtimes are busy, so a weekday morning is easier.
text.geographic_location: St Stephen's Green is in Dublin city centre, beside the Grafton Street shopping area. It sits among the city's Georgian streets, close to Merrion Square and Fitzwilliam Square.
text.directions_text: Take the Luas Green Line to the St. The Dawson stop on the Luas Green Line is about 7 minutes on foot away. From either stop, head for the park's edge and follow it to the arch entrance. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the arch and the path both fit naturally. If the arch is cut off, step back or switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep the path straight to avoid stretched edges. The telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is useful for a tighter shot of the far end of the path.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (at the arch entrance, looking south down the central path). The long, tree-lined central path running down through the park, framed by the arch in the foreground. If you want a second view, walk to the lake side of the park for the lake, stone bridges, waterfowl, flowerbeds and trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the path in the middle of the frame, with the arch making a border at the top and sides. Hold the phone at chest height and keep it level so the trees do not lean. For a calmer alternative to the main path, try the lake side of the park, where the bridges and water give a softer scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the far end of the path, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky or bright path looks washed out. Try a Live Photo if people are walking through, so you can pick the cleanest moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, just after sunrise, is the best time: one photographer found the light very good then. Weekday mornings are usually quieter, while sunny weekends and lunchtimes are busy.

text.access_note: St Stephen's Green is a public park run by the Office of Public Works; casual phone photos are fine, but professional or commercial shoots may need a permit, so check the official site before you go.

name: St Patrick's Cathedral
label: St Patrick's Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'St Patrick's Park' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Saint Patrick's Park' (way/19830551): middle (169 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/43981182: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Saint Patrick's Cathedral' (102 m across).

text.description: St Patrick's Cathedral is the national cathedral of the Church of Ireland, and the biggest church in Ireland. The main building dates from between 1191 and 1270, though little of the earliest work survives. The tower, known as Minot's Tower, and the west nave were rebuilt between 1362 and 1370 after a fire. Jonathan Swift, the writer, is the best-known dean. The cathedral photographs well because the tower and spire stand tall above a calm green setting, so you can include lawn, paths and fountain below them. The best free view is from St Patrick's Park, on the cathedral's north side. From here you see the long north flank with the square tower and spire rising over the lawn, and the fountain and paths make a natural foreground. Guides describe the park as the best place to photograph the cathedral from outside. Fit the whole building in from a little way back, then step closer for details such as the stonework and windows. If you want something quieter, Patrick Street gives a street-level view of the cathedral as you approach. People often walk through the park, so wait a moment for a clear gap, or use them to give a sense of scale. Keep your phone straight so the tower doesn't lean.
text.geographic_location: St Patrick's Cathedral is in the old part of Dublin south of the River Liffey, with St Patrick's Park on its north side. Christ Church Cathedral is about 400 metres away.
text.directions_text: From the St. Stephen's Green stop on the Luas Green Line, the cathedral is about 680 m away, to the west. From the Four Courts stop on the Luas Red Line, it is about 820 m away, to the south. Once there, go into St Patrick's Park on the cathedral's north side and stand by the fountain. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole north flank with the tower and spire. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want a lot of lawn and the fountain in front. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the tower and spire.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in St Patrick's Park (north side of the cathedral, by the fountain). The cathedral's north flank and square tower and spire rising over the park lawn, with the fountain and paths in the foreground. From here the cathedral lies to the south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it stands straight. Put the fountain or a curve of the path low in the frame to lead the eye towards the cathedral. If you want a quieter alternative, Patrick Street gives a street-level view of the cathedral's exterior as you approach it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the cathedral stone to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky turns white. Take one shot at 1x and one zoomed in on the tower, so you have both options.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or later in the day is usually calmer, with fewer people crossing the lawn. Soft, even light on a bright overcast day also suits the stonework.

text.access_note: St Patrick's Park is free to walk into, but check the official site before you go for park opening times, and for cathedral entry and photography rules, as the inside charges a fee and photography is not allowed during services.
claims_not_in_sources: The north side of the cathedral gets little direct sun, so the stone can look dark against a bright sky.
Early morning or later in the day is usually quieter in the park.
Soft, even light on a bright overcast day suits the stonework.
Park opening times may vary, so visitors should check them.

name: Ha'penny Bridge
label: Ha'penny Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Wellington Quay' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Wellington Quay nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/399007550: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ha'penny Bridge' (59 m across).

text.description:
The Ha'penny Bridge is a slim, white cast-iron footbridge with a single low arch over the River Liffey, linking the Temple Bar side of the river with the north quays. It was opened in May 1816 as the Wellington Bridge. Its iron ribs were cast in England in 18 sections and shipped to Dublin. For its first hundred years or so, the operator could charge a ha'penny toll to cross, and the toll was dropped in 1919. Its official name is now the Liffey Bridge, though almost everyone uses the nickname.

It photographs well because the arch is simple and graceful, and the colourful buildings along the opposite quay make a ready-made backdrop. From the south bank you see the arch in profile with those façades behind it, which is the angle most visitors want. After dark, the bridge lights and quay lights reflect in the river, which gives a second, quite different picture.

On a phone, keep it simple: stand back a little, use the default lens (1x), and let the arch fill the lower half of the frame. Midday is very crowded, so early morning or late evening gives you cleaner shots. The steps at the bridge ends can be steep and slippery, so watch your footing when you walk across.
text.geographic_location: The bridge crosses the River Liffey in central Dublin, between the Temple Bar side on the south bank and the north quays.
text.directions_text: The nearest Luas stop is Jervis (Luas Red Line), about 3 minutes on foot, with the bridge to the south-east of the stop. Westmoreland (Luas Green Line) is about 4 minutes on foot, with the bridge to the west. From either stop, walk to the south bank of the Liffey. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the arch in profile with the quayside façades behind it. Try the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter crop of the arch and the buildings opposite. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close and want the whole bridge and the sky, and keep the arch away from the edges, where it can stretch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Wellington Quay (south bank, Temple Bar side). The bridge's arch in profile with the colourful quayside façades on the opposite bank behind it. The bridge is to the north of you. From here you see the arch in profile with the colourful façades on the opposite bank behind it, which is the classic postcard angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the arch along the lower third, with the façades filling the middle and a little sky above. Wait for gaps in the walkers if you want a clean arch. For a different view, try Bachelors Walk on the north bank, looking back at the arch with the Temple Bar buildings rising behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the arch to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the white ironwork is not washed out. After dark, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on something steady, such as the quay wall, to keep the lights and reflections sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late evening, when crowds are thinner. After dark the bridge and quay lights reflect in the river, which makes a very different picture.

text.access_note: The bridge is a free, pedestrian-only crossing and the viewpoints are open public streets, so there is no ticket to buy; check the official site before you go if you need up-to-date access details.
claims_not_in_sources: Resting your elbows on a wall helps keep a night-mode shot steady on a phone.
Dropping the exposure slider helps keep sky detail and stops white ironwork looking washed out.

name: Christ Church Cathedral
label: Christ Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Christchurch Place' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Christchurch Place nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/27291101: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Christ Church Cathedral' (73 m across).

text.description:
Christ Church Cathedral is the older of Dublin's two medieval cathedrals, and it sits on high ground above the old Viking settlement at Wood Quay. It was founded in the early 11th century, rebuilt in stone in the late 12th century and heavily restored in the late 19th century. That restoration gave it the look you see today, including the tower, the flying buttresses and the covered footbridge. Because the surrounding medieval streets were swept away by road building, the cathedral now stands out on its own, which makes it easier to photograph as a single building.

The challenge is getting all of it in. Close to the front, the façade is too big for one frame and you end up pointing your phone upwards, so the walls lean inwards. Stepping back across the street, to Christchurch Place, solves this. If you have a few minutes, try a second angle from Winetavern Street, where the cathedral and Dublinia can be seen through the arch of the footbridge. Once you have your wide view, move in for details of the stonework and the buttresses. It is a working place of worship, so keep clear of services and doorways.
text.geographic_location: Christ Church Cathedral stands in the old medieval heart of Dublin, next to Wood Quay at the end of Lord Edward Street.
text.directions_text: The nearest tram stop is Four Courts on the Luas Red Line. From there the cathedral is to the south, about 7 minutes on foot. Smithfield on the Luas Red Line is a little further, about 10 minutes on foot, with the cathedral to the south-east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from across the street so the whole front and tower fit. If the pavement is crowded and you cannot step back far enough, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for tower and stonework details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Christchurch Place (step back from the cathedral front, across the street). The whole Gothic and Victorian façade with its tower, framed from a distance so the full building fits in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line up the tower with a vertical line. Hold the phone level, at chest height, rather than tilting it up, to stop the walls leaning inwards. Leave a little space around the building so it is not cramped. For a different view, walk to Winetavern Street and frame the cathedral and Dublinia through the arch of the footbridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the pale stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a touch so the sky does not wash out. Take a second shot at 2x or 3x for details of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day is usually calmer, with fewer people and less traffic in the frame. Soft, even light on a bright overcast day also suits the pale stonework.

text.access_note: The cathedral is a working place of worship and a visitor attraction, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and photography rules, as photography is not allowed during services and commercial photography needs written permission.
claims_not_in_sources: Standing back across the street lets the whole building fit in one phone frame, and from close up the walls lean inwards if you tilt the phone up.
Early in the day there are usually fewer people and less traffic.
Soft overcast light suits pale stonework.
Pavements near the cathedral can be crowded enough to need the ultra-wide lens.

name: Royal Hospital Kilmainham
label: Royal Hospital
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Military Road' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Military Road nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/41685963: large area 'Royal Hospital Kilmainham' (792 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
The Royal Hospital Kilmainham is a long, formal 17th-century building with a clock tower rising above its roofline. It was built between 1679 and 1687 as a home for retired soldiers, and it was modelled on Les Invalides in Paris. It is described as the first large classical building in Ireland, and it is one of the few 17th-century buildings in Dublin still standing. Since 1984 it has housed the Irish Museum of Modern Art, and its grounds are also used for concerts and events.

The building photographs well because of how you arrive. From Military Road, near the East Gate, a stone gate opens onto a tree-lined lane that climbs toward the hospital, and the clock-towered building sits at the top of the rise. That gives you a ready-made frame: the gate and trees around the edges, the lane leading the eye, and the building as the reward. It is a quieter, more atmospheric picture than the straight-on view of the long north facade. If you have time, the facade with its central pedimented porch is a good second shot from the grounds.

The approach is steep on foot, so take your time and stop at the bottom for your first picture, then again partway up for a tighter one. Keep the phone level so the gateposts and tree trunks stay upright.
text.geographic_location: The Royal Hospital Kilmainham is in Kilmainham, Dublin 8, on the west side of the city centre. It stands on Military Road, close to Phoenix Park.
text.directions_text: The nearest stops are James's and Rialto, both on the Luas Red Line. From James's it is about 475 m, heading west, and from Rialto it is about 630 m, heading north. Expect the last stretch up toward the building to be uphill. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the gate, the lane and the building all fit in one frame. Switch to 2x if you want the building to look closer and the trees to feel more tightly packed around the lane. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you stand very close to the gate and want the whole arch in the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Military Road (near the East Gate, looking up the tree-lined approach toward the building). The stone gate and the lane climbing toward the hospital, framing the clock-towered building at the top of the rise.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the lane along the centre line, with the clock tower near the top. Let the gate and the trees form a natural frame at the sides. For a different view, walk up to the grounds and photograph the long north facade with its central porch and clock tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out. Shaded lanes can look dark, so check the trees keep some detail. Take a few frames as you walk up the lane, since the view changes with each step.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually suits the stonework and avoids harsh shadows under the trees. A quieter time of day makes it easier to take the shot without people in the lane.

text.access_note: The grounds and approach are on a public street, but parts of the building and its tours may be ticketed or closed at times, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually suits the stonework and avoids harsh shadows under the trees.
A quieter time of day makes it easier to avoid people in the lane.
Walking from the Luas stops ends with an uphill stretch toward the building.

name: Iveagh Gardens
label: Iveagh Gardens
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Iveagh Gardens sunken lawns and fountains' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/275449345: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Iveagh Gardens' (333 m across).

text.description:
Iveagh Gardens is a quiet, formal public park tucked behind the buildings near the National Concert Hall, so it feels like a surprise after the busy streets around it. The gardens were laid out by Ninian Niven in 1865, in a style that sits between French formal and English landscape. That mix is why they photograph so well: clipped lawns and fountains in the middle, and softer, wilder planting at the edges.

The classic view is across the sunken lawns, where statues stand in fountains with trees closing in behind and bright green grass in front. It is a simple, layered scene that works well on a phone. If you have time, two other corners are worth a look. The cascade is a tumble of water over rockwork, framed by ivy and ferns. Its rocks are said to come from all 32 counties of Ireland. The rosarium is good for close-ups of pink and magenta roses in even light.

The gardens are almost surrounded by buildings, which is why many people walk past without noticing them. They were given to the Irish nation in 1939, with the wish that they stay unbuilt on.

Take your time and walk the whole garden before you choose a spot. Keep the fountain statue off-centre and let the trees frame it. Drones are not allowed, and professional or commercial shoots need permission from the gardens.
text.geographic_location: Iveagh Gardens sits in Dublin city centre, just south of St Stephen's Green, between Clonmel Street and Upper Hatch Street. It is next to the National Concert Hall and a short way off Harcourt Street.
text.directions_text: The nearest tram stop is Harcourt Luas stop on the Luas Green Line, about 4 minutes on foot, with the gardens to the north-east. From St. Stephen's Green Luas stop (also Luas Green Line) it is about 7 minutes on foot, heading south. The entrances are on Clonmel Street and Hatch Street, both off Harcourt Street. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the fountain, statue and trees together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in more of the lawn and sky. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for statue detail or the roses.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on the grass of the sunken formal panels, facing one of the fountain statues. From here your photo shows a statue standing in a fountain, with trees framing the background and bright green lawn in the foreground. Look at the map to find the exact spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the statue on one of the vertical lines rather than dead centre. Keep the lawn in the lower third and let the trees fill the sides. For a different view, try the cascade, with water tumbling over rockwork framed by ivy and ferns. The rosarium is good for close-up flower shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the statue to set focus and exposure, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or the water looks washed out. For the cascade, try Live Photos to catch the movement of the water. Hold the phone steady with both hands, and wipe the lens first.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a dry day in spring or summer, when the lawns are at their greenest, and aim for morning or late afternoon for softer light. Avoid June and September if you can, as parts of the gardens may be restricted around festival set-up and takedown.

text.access_note: This is a free public park, entered from Clonmel Street or Hatch Street; opening hours can vary, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late afternoon light is usually softer and more flattering for photos than midday sun.
Trees may cast patchy shade across the lawns on sunny days, so exposure may need adjusting.
Walking times of about 4 and 7 minutes are calculated from the distances to the Luas stops (distance x 1.3 / 80 m per minute).
Spring and summer are when the lawns and roses are likely to look their best.

name: Spire of Dublin
label: The Spire
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'O'Connell Street Lower' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of O'Connell Street Lower nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Spire of Dublin'.

text.description:
The Spire is a slim stainless steel needle, 120 metres tall, standing on O'Connell Street in the middle of Dublin. It replaced Nelson's Pillar, which was bombed in 1966, and it was designed by Ian Ritchie. It is a long cone about 3 metres across at the base, narrowing to just 15 centimetres at the top. The lower 10 metres carry a pattern based on a rock core sample and the DNA double helix. At dusk the base is lit, and the top 10 metres glow through thousands of tiny LED holes.

It photographs well because it is so simple. One clean vertical line rises above the street, and the shot-peened stainless steel catches the light. From the southern end of O'Connell Street you can include the neoclassical front of the General Post Office (GPO) and the Georgian-scale buildings on both sides. These frame the Spire neatly. A wider view from O'Connell Bridge shows it against the skyline and the river. Henry Street gives a tighter, shopfront-lined view of it.

The street is busy with people, buses and trams for most of the day, so early morning is much easier for a clear frame. Keep your phone zipped away between shots, as one guide warns of pickpockets in the busy midday hours.
text.geographic_location: The Spire stands in the O'Connell Street pedestrian zone, where the street meets Henry Street and North Earl Street. The GPO and O'Connell Bridge are nearby on O'Connell Street.
text.directions_text: The Marlborough Luas stop on the same line is about 3 minutes on foot, with the Spire to the west of it. Once you are on O'Connell Street, the Spire is easy to spot because it towers over everything around it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit the whole Spire and the street in one frame. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the GPO and both sides of the street included. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the patterned base or the glowing tip.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on O'Connell Street Lower (southern end, shooting north toward the Spire). The full height of the Spire rising up the street, with the GPO's neoclassical facade on one side and Georgian-scale buildings on both sides. From here the full height of the Spire rises up the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the Spire on a vertical line, a little off-centre, so the street leads the eye up to it. Hold the phone level and step back rather than tilting it up, as tilting makes the buildings lean inwards. For an alternative, go to O'Connell Bridge for the Spire against the skyline and river, or to Henry Street for it framed at the end of the shopfronts.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the Spire to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the steel. At dusk, use night mode and hold still to keep the lit top sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before about 7am, when the street is least crowded. Dusk is also worth a visit, when the base and the top of the Spire are lit.

text.access_note: The Spire is a free monument in an open pedestrian area, so there are no tickets to buy, but check the official site before you go if you need confirmation.
claims_not_in_sources: Tilting a phone upwards makes tall buildings appear to lean inwards.
The Marlborough Luas stop is about 3 minutes' walk and the O'Connell - GPO stop about 2 minutes' walk from the stand-here point (calculated from the stated distances).

name: Henrietta Street
label: Henrietta Street
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bolton Street' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Bolton Street and Henrietta Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/4396064: the middle of the OpenStreetMap line 'Henrietta Street' (120 m long).

text.description:
Henrietta Street is a short, very wide Georgian street on Dublin's north side, and it is a good place to photograph if you like long red-brick terraces. It was laid out by Luke Gardiner in the 1720s and is described as the earliest Georgian street in the city. Its width is unusual for an 18th-century street, so the big townhouses have room to breathe and you can see them properly. The street is a cul-de-sac, with the Law Library of King's Inns facing down it from the western end.

The houses were built for wealthy families but later became tenements. By 1911 there were 835 people living in just 15 of them. Restoration work has gone on in recent decades, and the street has been used as a period setting for film and television. Number 14 is now a museum.

The corner building sits close beside you and the terrace recedes away from you, which gives a strong sense of depth. This is a quieter spot than the middle of the street. For a second view, walk a little way in and shoot the full length of the terrace towards King's Inns. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines of the brickwork stay straight.
text.geographic_location: Henrietta Street is on the north side of Dublin city centre, just north of Bolton Street. It runs up to the Law Library of King's Inns at its western end.
text.directions_text: From the Broadstone - University stop on the Luas Green Line, walk south-east for about 4 minutes on foot to reach the street. From the Dominick stop on the Luas Green Line, walk north-west for about 6 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the corner building and the street receding away from you. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the corner and the sky, but stay square-on so the buildings don't lean. A telephoto of 2x or more suits pulling the terrace together.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Bolton Street and Henrietta Street (corner at the southeast end of Henrietta Street). The corner building and the mouth of Henrietta Street, with the street receding away from you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the corner building's edge with a vertical line. Let the row of fronts lead the eye down the street. For a different view, step into the street and shoot the full terrace towards King's Inns at the far end.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brickwork to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky looks washed out. Wait for a gap in passing people and traffic before you shoot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime is easiest. Soft, even light, such as on a bright overcast day, tends to suit red brick.

text.access_note: The street itself is a public street; number 14 is a museum and King's Inns has its own access rules, so check the official sites before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft, even light on a bright overcast day tends to suit red brick.
The Bolton Street corner is usually quieter than the middle of the street.
King's Inns is generally closed to visitors, with only the grounds open in daylight, and access may change.
Number 14 Henrietta Street is a paid museum.

name: Samuel Beckett Bridge
label: Samuel Beckett Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sir John Rogerson's Quay' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Sir John Rogerson's Quay nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/381481630: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Samuel Beckett Bridge' (132 m across).

text.description: Samuel Beckett Bridge crosses the River Liffey in the Docklands and joins Sir John Rogerson's Quay on the south bank to North Wall Quay and Guild Street on the north. The architect Santiago Calatrava led the design. It is a cable-stayed swing bridge: one tall, curved, tapering pylon holds up the deck with 31 cable stays. The shape of the pylon and cables is said to recall a harp lying on its side, and the harp has been Ireland's national symbol since at least the thirteenth century. That clean, simple outline is what makes it so easy to photograph on a phone. The bridge opened to pedestrians on 10 December 2009 and is named after the Irish writer Samuel Beckett. The steel span was built in Rotterdam, and the bridge can swing open through 90 degrees to let ships pass. The best view is side-on from the south quay, a little east of the bridge, where you get the whole span, the pylon and the fan of cables in one frame. On a clear day the dome of the Custom House sits behind it. The bridge looks its best at dusk or after dark, when it is lit. It can open to river traffic, so stay on the pavement and keep well back from the edge of the quay while you take your photos.
text.geographic_location: In Dublin's Docklands, crossing the River Liffey between Sir John Rogerson's Quay on the south bank and North Wall Quay on the north bank. It is east of the city centre, close to the Luas Red Line stops at Mayor Square - NCI and Spencer Dock.
text.directions_text: Take the Luas Red Line to Mayor Square - NCI, which is about 300 m from the bridge; the bridge lies to the south-east of the stop. Spencer Dock, also on the Luas Red Line, is about 350 m from the bridge, with the bridge to the south-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit the full span, the pylon and the cable fan in one frame. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the quay is busy and you can't step back far enough. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the pylon and cables, or to pull the Custom House dome in closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Sir John Rogerson's Quay (south bank, about 40 m east of the bridge). The bridge seen side-on with its single pylon and cable fan, with the Custom House dome behind on a clear day. For the side-on view of the whole span, with its single pylon and cable fan, move a little east along the quay.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and set the pylon on one of the vertical lines, with the deck running along the lower horizontal line. Keep the phone level so the deck doesn't slope. If you want a different view, North Wall Quay, on the far bank, shows the curved harp shape against the Docklands skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pylon to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays rich and the bridge doesn't blow out. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body, or rest the phone on a solid ledge, to keep the lit cables sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk or after dark, when the bridge is lit, and a clear day if you want the Custom House dome visible behind it.

text.access_note: The quays are open public streets and pavements, but the bridge can open to river traffic, so check the official site before you go if you are planning around a swing.

name: Merrion Square and the Georgian doors
label: Merrion Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Merrion Square' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Merrion Square West' (way/1086316926): point nearest the subject (143 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/4078069: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Merrion Square Park' (443 m across).

text.description: Merrion Square is a Georgian garden square whose original houses largely survive. Three sides are lined with redbrick townhouses, and the railed park sits in the middle. The photo here is the doors: a long row of bright front doors, each with its own fanlight and iron railings, with the trees of the park behind. The square was laid out in 1762, and the surrounding houses were largely finished by the early 1800s. Most are now offices rather than homes, but all the original 18th-century houses survive except Antrim House. Oscar Wilde lived at No. 1 and W. B. Yeats at No. 82, and the park has a statue of Wilde. For the doors, the south side terraces are the one to try first, looking along the row, and the east side is also recommended. Guides disagree about which side is best, so walk round and see which has the best light when you arrive. The doors belong to private homes and offices, so photograph from the public pavement and don't block any entrance. If you have time, Mount Street Upper shows a line of Georgian doors running towards the spire of the Pepper Canister church, and Fitzwilliam Street is quieter for unhurried shots. On Sundays, art stalls along the park railings can get in the way of your view.
text.geographic_location: Merrion Square is a Georgian garden square on the south side of Dublin city centre. Its west side backs onto the grounds of Leinster House, the National Gallery and the Natural History Museum.
text.directions_text: From Dawson (Luas Green Line), head south-east; it is about 650 m to the park centre. From St. Stephen's Green (Luas Green Line), head east; it is about 800 m to the park centre. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a row of doors with the park behind. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is too narrow to fit the row in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a single door, a fanlight or the railings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Merrion Square (south side terraces, looking along the row of doors (east side also recommended)). A row of brick Georgian townhouses with coloured doors, fanlights and railings, framed by the leafy park. The east side is also worth a look if you have time.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use them to keep the door frames and the edge of the terrace upright. Stand slightly to one side so the row of doors recedes into the distance, and let one colourful door sit near a grid line as your main subject. Keep to the public pavement and leave entrances clear. For a quieter alternative, try Mount Street Upper, where the line of doors leads the eye to the Pepper Canister church spire.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap a door to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the colours stay rich and the sky doesn't wash out. For a close-up of a fanlight, use telephoto rather than walking up to the door.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning before 9am, when the streets are quiet, or late afternoon, when sun falls on the doorways.

text.access_note: The park is a public park and the pavements are open, but the doors belong to private homes and offices, so stay on the pavement; check the official site before you go for any park closures.
claims_not_in_sources: Gridlines help keep door frames and building edges upright in the photo.
Lowering the exposure slightly can help keep door colours rich and avoid a washed-out sky.
Mount Street Upper and Fitzwilliam Street are a short walk from the square.

name: General Post Office
label: GPO
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'General Post Office' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'General Post Office' (relation/289528): middle (149 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/13894872988: the OpenStreetMap point 'General Post Office'.

text.description:
The General Post Office, or GPO, sits in the middle of O'Connell Street, Dublin's main thoroughfare, and is one of Ireland's most famous buildings. Francis Johnston designed it, the foundation stone was laid on 12 August 1814, and it opened for business on 6 January 1818. It is best known as the headquarters of the leaders of the 1916 Easter Rising. Patrick Pearse read out the Proclamation of the Irish Republic outside it on 24 April 1916. Fire gutted the building during the Rising, but the granite façade survived, and the interior was not rebuilt until 1929.

It photographs well because the front is so orderly. A portico of six fluted Ionic columns, about 24 metres wide, stands in pale Portland stone against the darker granite behind. Three statues stand along the top of the pediment: Mercury, Hibernia in the centre, and Fidelity. The columns are still marked by bullet damage, which is a good detail for a close shot. In front, the street keeps moving, so you can get buses, trams and people crossing the frame with the building behind them.

The whole front is about 67 metres long, so step back to fit it in. Keep your phone level so the columns stay upright. If you want a second angle, O'Connell Street Upper gives a street-level view down the street with the GPO, the Metropole and trams in the frame.
text.geographic_location: The GPO is in the centre of O'Connell Street Lower in Dublin city centre. It stands just north-west of the Abbey Street area and close to the Spire.
text.directions_text: The nearest stop is O'Connell - GPO on the Luas Green Line. The GPO is to the north-west and about 1 minute on foot. From Abbey Street on the Luas Red Line, walk north-west for about 3 minutes. The building is on O'Connell Street and is hard to miss. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full width of the front and the street. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of the portico. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the statues on the pediment and the bullet-marked columns.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on General Post Office (front steps, facing O'Connell Street Lower). The neoclassical portico and façade of the GPO with O'Connell Street and its passing traffic in front of it. From there the building is to the east, with the portico and façade framed by O'Connell Street and its passing traffic. The front steps are also a good place to watch the street, and a guide says they are free to stand on at any time.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the columns up with the vertical lines so the façade does not lean. Keep the portico central, with a strip of street and passing traffic in the foreground. If you want the whole width, step back and use 0.5x, but keep the building away from the edges of the frame, where it stretches. For a different view, try the street-level angle from O'Connell Street Upper, with the Metropole and trams in the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone façade to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is washing out. Try a Live Photo to catch a tram or bus passing, then choose the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight shows the portico and statues best. Check how the light falls on the day, as the façade can be in shade at some times.

text.access_note: The front steps and the street outside are open public space, but check the official site before you go if you want to visit inside the building.
claims_not_in_sources: The stand-here point is on the O'Connell Street side, looking east to the portico.
The façade faces west onto O'Connell Street, so it can be in shade at some times of day.
Trams and buses regularly pass along O'Connell Street in front of the building.
The Metropole is visible in the view from O'Connell Street Upper (given in the researched viewpoint notes).

name: Dublin City Hall
label: City Hall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Parliament Street' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Parliament Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/25631284: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Dublin City Hall' (53 m across).

text.description:
Dublin City Hall began life as the Royal Exchange, a meeting place for the city's merchants. It was built between 1769 and 1779 to a design by Thomas Cooley, and it is a fine example of 18th-century neo-classical architecture. Today it is the formal seat of Dublin City Council. It sits on a slope on Dame Street, at the southern end of Parliament Street, in front of part of Dublin Castle. That makes it a handsome sight when you look down the street towards it.

The front is faced in pale Portland stone and topped by a green copper dome, so it stands out clearly against the busy street. It works especially well as a backdrop for a portrait of a friend or a travelling companion. A wedding photographer recommends Parliament Street for exactly this, and warns that you will need to wait for a gap in the traffic. Take care near the road and never step out for the shot. Wait on the pavement until the road is clear.

If the street is too busy, try the City Hall steps for a closer view of the entrance. Another option is Capel Street Bridge, where City Hall appears in the distance down the quays. The steps may be crowded with wedding guests on event days.
text.geographic_location: City Hall is on Dame Street on the south side of the Liffey, at the southern end of Parliament Street. It stands right in front of part of Dublin Castle.
text.directions_text: From the Jervis stop on the Luas Red Line, walk about 450 m south to reach Parliament Street and the building. From the Four Courts stop on the Luas Red Line, head about 530 m south-east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a portrait with the whole front of City Hall behind your subject. Try 2x if you want to stay well back on the pavement and still fill the frame. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you need the full width of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Parliament Street (looking toward the building from the street, with the traffic gap noted by the source). City Hall's front facade framed as the backdrop for a portrait taken from the street. Keep to the pavement and wait for a gap in the traffic before you take the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put your subject slightly off-centre so the columns and the green dome show behind them. Switch on the gridlines to keep the building upright. As an alternative, you could try the view from Capel Street Bridge, where City Hall appears in the distance down the quays.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on your subject to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale stone and sky do not wash out. Portrait mode suits people shots, but check that the edges of the building still look natural.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the traffic is lighter, so you get more clear gaps, and the pavement is less crowded. Check the building and steps for wedding parties on event days.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the public street, but check the official site before you go if you want to go inside or visit the exhibition.
claims_not_in_sources: Traffic and pedestrian crowds are usually lighter early in the morning.
Parliament Street has a pavement where you can wait for a gap in the traffic.
The building's front faces north up Parliament Street, so direct sun seldom lights it.

name: The Custom House
label: Custom House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sir John Rogerson's Quay' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Sir John Rogerson's Quay nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/610966: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'The Custom House' (135 m across).

text.description: The Custom House is a neoclassical building on the north bank of the Liffey, designed by James Gandon and opened for business on 7 November 1791. Its long river front, columns and central dome make it one of the easiest buildings in Dublin to photograph across the water. The facades carry sculptures by Edward Smyth representing Ireland's rivers, though from the south bank you will mostly see the overall shape. The building was burnt in 1921 and the dome collapsed. When it was restored, the new dome was made from Irish Ardbraccan limestone, which is noticeably darker than the original stone. In a photo you can see that change in colour for yourself. The best view is from the south bank, on Sir John Rogerson's Quay, near the approach to the Samuel Beckett Bridge. From there the full width of the river facade sits under the dome, with the river in front. If you want something closer, Custom House Quay gives a nearer view of the riverfront with its reflection on calm water, and Talbot Memorial Bridge shows the facade along the river. The Custom House is a government building, so it is best treated as an exterior shot. Keep the building central, keep the quay railing or footpath out of the bottom of the frame, and wait for gaps in the passers-by.
text.geographic_location: On the north bank of the River Liffey in Dublin city centre, on Custom House Quay between Butt Bridge and Talbot Memorial Bridge.
text.directions_text: For the building itself, get off at the Busáras stop on the Luas Red Line; it is about 3 minutes on foot to the Custom House, to the south-west. From the Marlborough stop on the Luas Green Line, the Custom House is to the east, about 5 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the whole river facade and dome in one frame. If the foreground looks empty or cluttered, try 2x to tighten the view. The ultra-wide (0.5x) tends to make the building look small and adds a lot of empty sky and water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Sir John Rogerson's Quay (south bank, near the Samuel Beckett Bridge approach). The full width of the Custom House's river facade with the Portland stone dome above, seen across the Liffey.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the base of the building with a horizontal line so the facade does not lean. Put the dome near the centre and leave a strip of river in the foreground. For a variation, try Custom House Quay for a closer view with the reflection, or Talbot Memorial Bridge for the facade along the river.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the stonework keeps its detail. If the water is calm, take a few shots, as the reflection is better when the surface is still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before about 09:00, is recommended for a quieter foreground. The river facade faces the water, so it is often well lit when the sun is out.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the public quays and bridges; the Custom House is a working government building and the visitor centre may restrict photos, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The river facade of the Custom House faces south towards the Liffey, so it is lit by the sun for much of the day when the sky is clear.
At roughly half a kilometre the building looks small in an ultra-wide shot, so the default lens (1x) or 2x works better.
Calm water gives a clearer reflection than a rippled surface.
